Neonates of the Jamaican opal-bellied anole emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after a developmental period of approximately 50 days [ab = approximately 50 days] when eggs are incubated at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. At the moment of hatching, these hatchlings exhibit a snout-vent length of 2.5 cm [Lb = 2.5 cm] and a corresponding wet weight of 0.36 grams [Wwb = 0.36 grams]. This modest body size at emergence is typical for many small-bodied anoles and reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the yolk-dependent embryo stage. Upon rupturing the chorion and completing the hatching event, the young individuals absorb the remaining yolk material over the first few days post-eclosion. The lecithotrophic larva then transitions to active feeding, marking the onset of exogenous feeding where they begin to capture small arthropods. Field observations suggest that this early life history phase is characterized by rapid growth as the juveniles exploit the abundant insect prey available in their humid forest floor habitat.

The growth trajectory of juvenile Anolis opalinus is strongly influenced by thermal conditions, with optimal development occurring at temperatures around 25 °C. Under these conditions, females progress through the juvenile stage and attain puberty at a snout-vent length of 3.7 cm [Lp = 3.7 cm]. This milestone of sexual maturation represents the onset of gonadal activation and the beginning of gametogenesis in the immature organism. Prior to this, growing juveniles must accumulate sufficient body reserves to support the energetic demands of reproductive activation. Comparative studies with related congeners such as Anolis gundlachi indicate that the timing of puberty in this species is closely tied to achieving this critical size threshold, after which females become capable of producing their first egg clutch. The pre-reproductive juvenile phase encompasses a period of considerable somatic investment, during which the young reptiles allocate resources primarily to structural growth and lipid storage. This strategy ensures that individuals are physiologically prepared for the rigors of breeding upon reaching the pubertal size.

Sexually mature adult females of Anolis opalinus attain a maximum recorded snout-vent length of 4.4 cm [Li = 4.4 cm], corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of 1.98 grams [Wwi = 1.98 grams]. Males, in contrast, exhibit a larger adult body size, reaching a final snout-vent length of 5.2 cm [Li = 5.2 cm] and a corresponding ultimate wet weight of 3.26 grams [Wwi = 3.26 grams]. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism is a common feature among anoline lizards and is typically attributed to sexual selection, where larger males enjoy advantages in territory acquisition and access to receptive females. The ultimate wet weight estimates for both sexes are derived from allometric relationships informed by data from Anolis gundlachi, scaled appropriately for the species-specific adult lengths. Reproductively active adults can be observed year-round in suitable habitats, with gravid females carrying a single, leathery-shelled egg in the oviduct at any given time, a reproductive mode known as single-egg clutching that is characteristic of many Anolis species.

The maximum reproductive rate for this species has been estimated based on studies conducted on its congener Anolis gundlachi at a controlled environmental temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. Under these thermal conditions, the data indicate that females can produce approximately 18 eggs over the course of a full year [Ri = approximately 18 eggs over the course of a full year]. This rate of egg production is expressed biologically as the maximum number of offspring a female can produce per year at that specific temperature, and it represents the upper limit of her reproductive output under favorable resource conditions. In natural populations, the actual laying rate may be lower due to factors such as food limitation, competition, and variable thermal microenvironments. The single-egg clutch pattern means that total annual fecundity is equivalent to the number of nesting events per year, as each reproductive event yields precisely one offspring. This life-history trait is thought to reduce the metabolic burden on the gravid female during locomotion and foraging.

The lifespan of Anolis opalinus under natural conditions has been documented to extend to a maximum of 7 years [am = 7 years] when measured at a constant ambient temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This longevity, recorded from mark-recapture studies in Jamaican forests, surpasses that of many smaller anole species and may be linked to the relatively stable tropical environment and low extrinsic mortality rates. Senescence in older individuals is marked by a gradual decline in reproductive output and a deterioration of physiological homeostasis. The completion of the lifespan, or biological death, typically occurs following multiple breeding seasons, with the oldest individuals often exhibiting signs of reproductive senescence before their final year. Field surveys have documented that very few individuals survive beyond the seventh year, suggesting that 7 years [am = 7 years] represents a reliable upper bound for maximum recorded longevity in this species at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan, combined with the single-egg clutching strategy, yields a relatively low lifetime reproductive output compared to other lizard families, reflecting the conservative life-history pace of the genus Anolis.
